routes.name: Triumphal route (Republican)

stops.t: Army and general assemble in the Campus Martius by the Villa Publica; the Senate meets in the Temple of Bellona to grant the triumph
Through the Circus Flaminius, where spoils and captives are displayed to the crowd
Porta Triumphalis: the general crosses the pomerium still holding his imperium
Enters the Circus Maximus at the starting gates; spectators line the stands
Leaves by the gate in the curved end
Turns north along the valley between Palatine and Caelian and onto the Sacra Via
Down through the Forum; prisoners like Jugurtha or Vercingetorix are led off to the Carcer to be killed
Sacrifice of white oxen to Jupiter Optimus Maximus; the general lays his laurel in the god's lap

scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
Coarelli, 'La Porta Trionfale e la Via dei Trionfi', DialArch 2 (1968)
Favro, 'The street triumphant', in Celik et al. (eds), Streets (1994)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
routes.note: Standard modern reconstruction (Coarelli, Beard). The exact place of the Porta Triumphalis is disputed: Coarelli puts it by the Temple of Fortuna Redux between the Circus Flaminius and the Forum Holitorium; others identify it with the Porta Carmentalis. Over 300 triumphs were celebrated in the Republic.

routes.name: Triumphal route (Imperial, after Josephus' account of AD 71)

stops.t: Vespasian and Titus spend the night by the Temple of Isis in the Campus Martius
At dawn they meet the Senate and equestrians in the Porticus Octaviae and receive the soldiers' acclamation
Breakfast and sacrifice by the Porta Triumphalis, then the procession passes 'through the theatres' (Marcellus) for the crowds
Through the Circus Maximus; later triumphs passed the Arch of Titus in its curved end (AD 81)
Past the Meta Sudans and the Colosseum (from 80), and from 315 the Arch of Constantine
Under the Arch of Titus on the Velia showing the spoils of Jerusalem
Simon bar Giora is executed at the Carcer while the procession halts
Sacrifice at the Capitoline Temple

sources.w: On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius

scholarship: Beard, The Roman Triumph (2007)
Coarelli, 'La Porta Trionfale e la Via dei Trionfi', DialArch 2 (1968)
Favro, 'The street triumphant', in Celik et al. (eds), Streets (1994)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
routes.note: Follows Josephus' eyewitness account of the Flavian triumph of 71. Last celebrated in full form in Rome by Diocletian and Maximian (303) and in a reduced form by Honorius (404).

routes.name: Pompa circensis

stops.t: The presiding magistrate in triumphal dress leads the procession from the Capitol
Through the Forum: the youths of the city on horse and foot, the charioteers, athletes, dancers in armour and satyr-mimes
Down the Vicus Tuscus, the street of the Etruscans
Enters the Circus Maximus by the starting gates
Rounds the far turning post; the images of the gods on litters and carriages (tensae) are set on the pulvinar
Back to the starting gates, where the races begin

scholarship: Latham, Performance, Memory, and Processions in Ancient Rome: The Pompa Circensis (2016)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
routes.note: Dionysius gives the order of the procession from Fabius Pictor. Route via the Forum and Vicus Tuscus is attested; the lap of the arena is assumed.

routes.name: Funeral of Augustus

stops.t: The body, brought from Nola by the equestrians and laid in the vestibule of his Palatine house, is carried out on an ivory and gold couch by the magistrates-elect
Before the Temple of Divus Iulius: Tiberius delivers the eulogy
At the old Rostra: Drusus reads the second eulogy
By Senate decree the cortege leaves through the Porta Triumphalis
Cremation at the ustrinum in the northern Campus Martius; an ex-praetor swears he saw Augustus' spirit rise to heaven; Livia stays five days to gather the bones
The ashes are laid in the Mausoleum

scholarship: Arce, Funus imperatorum (1988)
Price, 'From noble funerals to divine cult', in Cannadine and Price (eds), Rituals of Royalty (1987)
routes.note: Date: funeral in September AD 14 (Augustus died 19 August at Nola). Route between Forum and Campus inferred from the decree that the procession pass the Porta Triumphalis.

routes.name: Lupercalia run around the Palatine

stops.t: 15 February: sacrifice of goats and a dog at the Lupercal cave; two young men are smeared with the bloody knife and wiped with wool soaked in milk
Naked but for goatskin belts, the Luperci run round the Palatine striking women with thongs of goat hide to make them fertile
In the Forum: in 44 BC Antony, running as a Lupercus, offered Caesar a diadem at the Rostra
Return to the Lupercal

scholarship: Wiseman, 'The god of the Lupercal', JRS 85 (1995)
North, 'Caesar at the Lupercalia', JRS 98 (2008)
routes.note: Ancient authors describe the course as a circuit of the Palatine (a purification of Romulus' city) or as running up and down the Sacra Via; this line combines both. Pope Gelasius I attacked the festival around 494; it is not heard of afterwards.

routes.name: Procession of the Argei

stops.t: 16-17 March: visits begin at the shrines of the Suburana region on the Caelian
Esquilina region: shrines on the Oppius, Fagutal and Cispius
Collina region: shrines on the Quirinal and Viminal
Palatina region: shrines on the Velia, Cermalus and Palatine
14-15 May: the Vestals, pontiffs and praetors throw 27 straw figures (Argei) from the Pons Sublicius into the Tiber

scholarship: Palmer, The Archaic Community of the Romans (1970)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Argeorum Sacraria
routes.note: Varro preserves extracts from the pontifical lists of the 27 sacraria of the Argei, region by region; only the order of regions and hills is known, so the line through them is schematic. The May rite at the Pons Sublicius is well attested.

routes.name: Ludi Saeculares of 17 BC

stops.t: Nights of 31 May-2 June: Augustus sacrifices at the Tarentum by the Tiber to the Moirai, the Ilithyiae and Terra Mater; Agrippa joins him
Days 1 and 2: white bulls to Jupiter and a white cow to Juno on the Capitol; 110 matrons hold sellisternia
Day 3: sacrifice to Apollo and Diana at the Palatine temple; 27 boys and 27 girls sing Horace's Carmen Saeculare
The hymn is sung again on the Capitol

scholarship: Schnegg-Köhler, Die augusteischen Säkularspiele (2002)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (2002)
routes.note: The inscribed acta (found 1890 near the Tarentum) record the programme. Movement between the sites is reconstructed along the main streets.

routes.name: Entry of Constantine (29 October 312)

stops.t: After the battle of 28 October Maxentius' body is pulled from the Tiber by the Milvian Bridge; his head is carried on a spear before the army
Through the Porta Flaminia; the Senate and people pour out to meet the victor
Down the Via Lata towards the Forum
The Forum and Senate house: Constantine promises to restore the Senate's dignity
He goes up to the Palatine palace; the panegyrist of 313 notes he did not climb the Capitol to sacrifice

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
MacCormack, Art and Ceremony in Late Antiquity (1981)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
routes.note: Route along the Via Flaminia and Via Lata is the natural one; the order of stops follows the Latin panegyric of 313.

routes.name: Visit of Theodoric to Rome (500)

stops.t: Pope Symmachus, the Senate and people meet the Arian king outside the city; he prays at St Peter's 'as devoutly as a Catholic'
Enters the city across the Tiber
Visits the Senate in the Curia
Addresses the people at the place called 'ad Palmam' in the Forum, promising to keep the laws of the emperors

Takes up residence in the Palatine palace; holds his tricennalia, gives circus games and grants 120,000 modii of grain a year to the poor and 200 pounds of gold a year for repairing the palace and walls

scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
routes.note: The Anonymus Valesianus gives the sequence of stops; the streets between them are reconstructed.

routes.name: Totila takes Rome (17 December 546)

stops.t: Four Isaurian guards let the Goths in through the Porta Asinaria at night
Through the deserted city: most of the starving population had already fled with Bessas' garrison
Totila goes to pray at St Peter's, where the deacon Pelagius begs him to spare the people; he threatens to raze Rome and turn it into pasture, and pulls down parts of the walls

scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
routes.note: Procopius reports the entry at the Porta Asinaria and the visit to St Peter's; the path between them is reconstructed along the main late-antique route. Procopius says the city was left without inhabitants for some time afterwards.

routes.name: Sevenfold litany of 590: procession of the clergy from Santi Cosma e Damiano

stops.t: The clergy gather at Santi Cosma e Damiano
All seven processions converge on Santa Maria Maggiore, singing Kyrie eleison

scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Markus, Gregory the Great and his World (1997)
routes.note: Gregory the Great, newly elected after Pope Pelagius II died of the plague, ordered seven processions to set out simultaneously from seven churches. Gregory of Tours heard from his deacon who was present that 80 people collapsed and died during the hour of the procession. The later legend of the angel sheathing his sword over Hadrian's Mausoleum is medieval. Streets between church and basilica reconstructed.

routes.name: Sevenfold litany of 590: procession of abbots and monks from Santi Gervasio e Protasio (San Vitale)

stops.t: Abbots and monks gather at Santi Gervasio e Protasio (San Vitale)
All seven processions converge on Santa Maria Maggiore, singing Kyrie eleison

scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Markus, Gregory the Great and his World (1997)

All seven processions converge on Santa Maria Maggiore, singing Kyrie eleison

All seven processions converge on Santa Maria Maggiore, singing Kyrie eleison

routes.name: Papal stational procession: Lateran to St Peter's

stops.t: The pope leaves the Lateran episcopium on horseback with his household and the clergy of the regions
Past the Colosseum
Through the Forum
Across the Campus Martius on the later Via Papalis
Mass at the station church, St Peter's

scholarship: Baldovin, The Urban Character of Christian Worship (1987)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
de Blaauw, Cultus et decor (1994)
routes.note: The stational liturgy, in which the bishop of Rome celebrated in a different church each day of Lent and the great feasts, took shape in the 5th-6th centuries; the people gathered at a collecta church and processed to the station. The route through Forum and Campus is that of the papal processions described in the Ordo Romanus I (c. 700) and later; its 6th-century course is assumed.

routes.name: Papal stational procession: Lateran to Santa Maria Maggiore

stops.t: Departure from the Lateran
Station at Santa Maria Maggiore (Christmas night, Easter Sunday, and the Marian feasts)

scholarship: Baldovin, The Urban Character of Christian Worship (1987)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
routes.note: Straight along the ridge of the Esquiline on the line of the later Via Merulana, the shortest link between the cathedral and the main Marian basilica built by Sixtus III (432-440).

routes.name: Litania maior (25 April): San Lorenzo in Lucina to St Peter's

stops.t: Gathering at San Lorenzo in Lucina
Across the Milvian Bridge
Down the Via Triumphalis to St Peter's

scholarship: Baldovin, The Urban Character of Christian Worship (1987)
routes.note: The Christianised Robigalia of 25 April: the old festival procession went out by the Via Flaminia; the Christian litany followed the same road and returned along the right bank to St Peter's. Attested in Gregory the Great's time; route after the Ordo of the 8th century.

routes.name: Funeral procession of Julius Caesar (March 44 BC)

stops.t: The body is carried by magistrates from the Domus Publica, his official house as pontifex maximus
Laid in a gilded shrine modelled on the Temple of Venus Genetrix before the Rostra; Antony's eulogy and the display of the bloodied toga and a wax effigy with the 23 wounds inflame the crowd
Instead of taking the bier to the pyre prepared in the Campus Martius by Julia's tomb, the crowd burns it in the Forum on benches and furniture; the Temple of Divus Iulius later rises on the spot

scholarship: Sumi, Ceremony and Power (2005)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
routes.note: Date c. 20 March 44 BC.

routes.name: Funeral of a Republican noble (pompa funebris)

stops.t: From the family house on the Palatine slope, preceded by musicians and mourners, actors wear the wax masks of the ancestors in the robes of their highest office
At the Rostra the 'ancestors' sit on ivory chairs while a son delivers the eulogy of the dead man and of each ancestor in turn
Out through the Porta Capena
Burial or cremation at the family tomb on the Via Appia, as at the Tomb of the Scipios

scholarship: Flower, Ancestor Masks and Aristocratic Power in Roman Culture (1996)
routes.note: Representative route of the aristocratic funeral described by Polybius; the house and tomb are examples.

routes.name: Flight and death of Gaius Gracchus (121 BC)

stops.t: Gracchus and Fulvius Flaccus hold the Aventine with their armed supporters; Gracchus withdraws to the Temple of Diana and is stopped by friends from killing himself
Down past the Porta Trigemina to the river as the consul Opimius' men with Cretan archers storm the hill
At the Pons Sublicius his friends Pomponius and Laetorius hold off the pursuers and are killed
In the grove of Furrina on the Janiculum his slave Philocrates kills him and then himself; his head is taken to Opimius for its weight in gold. About 3,000 of his followers are killed

scholarship: Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) s.v. Lucus Furrinae
routes.note: Route from the Aventine to the bridge and the Lucus Furrinae follows Plutarch and Orosius.

routes.name: Gallic advance into Rome (390 BC)

stops.t: Three days after the rout at the Allia the Gauls under Brennus come down the Via Salaria
They find the Porta Collina open and the city undefended
In the Forum the old senators sit in their doorways in their robes of office; M. Papirius strikes a Gaul who strokes his beard and the massacre begins. The city is burned
A night attempt to climb the Capitol near the shrine of Carmenta is foiled when Juno's geese wake M. Manlius
After a seven-month siege the Capitol's defenders pay a ransom of 1,000 pounds of gold

scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995)
Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001)
routes.note: Livy's account; the Greek historians date the sack to 387/386 BC. No archaeological destruction layer of this date has been securely identified. The wall of 378 BC did not yet exist.

routes.name: Alaric's Goths enter Rome (24 August 410)

stops.t: At night the gate of the Via Salaria is opened (by treachery or by the slaves of a noblewoman, according to rival stories)
The Goths burn the houses by the gate, including the old palace in the Gardens of Sallust
The Basilica Aemilia burns; bronze coins melted into its floor are still visible; the Secretarium Senatus is damaged
On the Aventine the rich houses are plundered; Marcella is beaten
The Goths respect the basilicas of Peter and Paul as asylum; sacred vessels are carried there in procession under guard

scholarship: Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City, 312-1308 (1980)
Lipps, Machado and von Rummel (eds), The Sack of Rome in 410 AD (2013)
routes.note: Three days of plunder. Entry by the Porta Salaria is in Procopius; the route down the Alta Semita to the Forum is reconstructed.
